minor: 'Rowe went to see them' (the Stones in Richmond): the listed sources only say Rowe heard of the band from Harrison and Decca signed them within days. Sources differ on whether Rowe or Mike Smith made the trip, so say 'Decca went to see them' or check Wyman.

'Epstein had helped pick the list, leaning on standards and covers to show range rather than the band's own sound': the source only says Epstein helped choose the set. The motive is interpretation, so attribute it ('biographers suggest') or cut it.
'a band an hour away can be in the studio whenever a song is ready': 'an hour' is not in the sources, and it is the script's own gloss on Smith's 'local' reasoning. Say 'a band nearby'.
'An engineer there liked the original songs': the source only says an engineer referred Epstein to Ardmore & Beechwood. The engineer's liking the songs is not documented in the list.

'They reached London late on the last night of 1961': the source gives the ten-hour snowy drive but no arrival time. Lewisohn has them getting lost, so soften to 'reached London that evening' unless the book confirms it.

'Five songs from the Decca audition were finally released on Anthology 1': this follows the listed source, but Anthology 1 is often described as carrying more Decca tracks. Verify the count against the liner notes.
'Decca came closest: it had the Beatles in its own studio': this is opinion. EMI/Parlophone did sign them, so word it as 'of the labels that said no, Decca came closest'.

'Seventy-three million Americans watched': Nielsen's figure is an estimate of viewers (it includes non-Americans only in the sense of non-US households not counted). This is fine as written, but 'an estimated' would be safer.
'Parlophone, one of EMI's smaller labels' and 'some of the biggest records of the decade' have no sources entry. They are descriptive, not figures.
